Keep the shape identical across backends so the rule is one rule, not five.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a backend_config value that is accepted but semantically destructive/unusable. Lift the sqlite corpus into a shared table-driven case run against every backend that takes `retention_days` (sqlite, redis, nats, postgres): for each of null, 0, -1, -0.5, NaN, Infinity, '30', '30d', true, {}, assert connect() rejects with an error naming the key AND that a pre-seeded history is still intact afterwards. packages/bridge-postgres/test/retention.test.ts is not merely too narrow - its first row (['prunes older rows when set', 0, 0]) asserts the destructive value is *correct*, so it must be changed to expect rejection.

summary: `prune()` computes `new Date(...).toISOString()` OUTSIDE its try block, so a non-numeric `retention_days` throws RangeError from an un-awaited async call - an unhandled promise rejection that kills the bridge process (Node's default), once at connect and again on every hourly tick.
failure: backend_config `{ retention_days: 'abc' }` (or Infinity) -> connect() resolves; the `void this.prune()` at index.ts:183 rejects with `RangeError: Invalid time value`. Reproduced live: vitest reported two `Unhandled Rejection: RangeError: Invalid time value` for the 'abc' and Infinity cells. Under the real CLI there is no handler, so an operator with a typoed retention window gets a bridge that dies at startup with a stack trace and no mention of the config key.
remediation: Validate `retention_days` at connect (see the previous finding) so this input never reaches prune; additionally move the cutoff computation inside prune()'s try, and give the `void this.prune()` / setInterval call sites a `.catch()`, so no best-effort background chore can ever become an unhandled rejection.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a best-effort background task whose failure escapes as an unhandled rejection. Parameterize over every fire-and-forget path in the plugin (prune tick, drain, reconnect, waiter re-check): install a `process.on('unhandledRejection')` spy, force each to throw (bad config value, pool that rejects, clock stub), and assert the spy is never called and the plugin still serves fetchRecent. Widen the generator to non-number config values rather than pinning 'abc'.

summary: `pool_size` is passed straight to `new Pool({ max })`. A negative value makes `pool.connect()` in the schema bootstrap never settle: connect() hangs forever with no error, no timeout and no log line.
failure: backend_config `{ url, table_name, pool_size: -3 }` -> `await plugin.connect(...)` never resolves. Reproduced live with a 4s race: `pool_size=-3 -> TIMEOUT connect` (0, 'abc' and 2.5 all connect and serve). In production the parley-postgres binary hangs before printing `bridge up`, so the MCP session sees a server that never initialises and never errors.
remediation: Validate `pool_size` in the same connect-time validator: require an integer >= 1 (and a sane ceiling), rejecting with a message that names the key. Fail fast beats a silent hang.
testUpgrade: CLASS = an unvalidated numeric knob that produces a hang rather than an error. Table-drive every numeric backend_config knob across backends (pool_size, poll_interval_ms, retention_days, any timeout) over [-1, 0, 0.5, NaN, Infinity, '5', null], asserting connect() either succeeds or rejects *within a bounded timeout* - the assertion must be Promise.race against a deadline so a hang fails the test instead of blowing the suite timeout ambiguously.

summary: `subscribe()` checks `this.subs.get(channel)` before two awaits (the MAX(seq) tail read and `acquireListen`) and only then does `this.subs.set(channel, sub)`. Two concurrent subscribes to the same topic both miss the existing-check, and the second overwrites the first: the first handler is silently dropped forever and the channel's LISTEN refcount is left at 2. The JSDoc at index.ts:88 claims the opposite ("a repeat subscribe appends ... so a second subscribe doesn't silently replace the first").
failure: `await Promise.all([p.subscribe(t, h1), p.subscribe(t, h2)]); await p.post(t, 'u', 'hello')` against live Postgres -> h1 receives 0 messages, h2 receives 1. Instrumentation printed `subs size 1, handlers [1], refs [2]`. Sequential awaits behave correctly, which is why nothing caught it.
remediation: Register the subscription synchronously before the first await (an in-flight entry keyed by channel that later subscribes append to and await), so the existing-check and the insertion are not separated by an await; on LISTEN failure remove the entry, preserving the BUG-29 property. Also release the extra listen ref taken on the losing path.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a check-then-act on a registry separated by an await (the same shape as the lost-wakeup family). Add a parameterized case to the shared conformance suite: for k in [2,3] and for each of {same topic, distinct topics}, call Promise.all(k subscribes) then post once, and assert EVERY handler received the message exactly once and the plugin's internal listen/refcount bookkeeping is at the expected value after disconnect. Run it against every backend - bridge-xmpp's append-on-repeat path has the identical shape. packages/bridge-postgres/test/lifecycle.test.ts's 'two subscribes to the same topic fan out' case awaits them sequentially and so can never see this.

summary: The reconnect matrix advertises a `DRAIN_BATCH + 1` (513-row) cell to cover the multi-batch drain, but the mock pool returns every queued row on the first SELECT regardless of the `LIMIT` in the SQL. The inner `for(;;)` re-query loop in `drain()` is therefore completely unguarded, and the live conformance suite never posts more than a handful of messages per subscription.
failure: Mutation test, run for real: I changed `LIMIT ${DRAIN_BATCH}` to `LIMIT 1` and collapsed the inner for(;;) loop to a single batch, then ran the whole package suite - 7 files / 153 tests still passed, including all six '513 row(s)' cells. Under that mutation a live blackout probe (kill the LISTEN backend, post 5 messages, reconnect) delivered only ['dark0']: 4 messages never reach the live path until some unrelated later post rings the doorbell.
remediation: Teach the mock pool to honour the `LIMIT n` it is handed (parse it and slice), so a batch-boundary regression fails; and add one live case that posts > DRAIN_BATCH messages during a listener blackout and asserts all of them arrive, in order, exactly once.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a fake that cannot express a server-side cap the code under test depends on. Audit every mocked query surface for caps the real server enforces (LIMIT, page size, payload size, per-call row cap) and make the fake enforce them; then table-drive the drain over row counts [0, 1, DRAIN_BATCH-1, DRAIN_BATCH, DRAIN_BATCH+1, 2*DRAIN_BATCH+3] in BOTH the mocked reconnect matrix and one live blackout test, asserting completeness, order and no duplicates.

summary: `connect()` reads four known keys off `backend_config` and ignores everything else, so a typo disables a feature with no error. bridge-sqlite explicitly rejects unknown keys for exactly this reason (index.ts:402).
failure: backend_config `{ url, table_name, retention_day: 30, poll_interval_ms: 500 }` -> connect() resolves normally (reproduced live: `typo keys -> accepted`). The operator believes retention is enforced and that they tuned the poll interval; neither key exists, nothing prunes, and nothing ever says so.
remediation: Add the unknown-key check from bridge-sqlite to the same connect-time validator: enumerate ['url','table_name','pool_size','retention_days'] and throw naming the offending key and the accepted set.
testUpgrade: CLASS = silent acceptance of unrecognised config. One shared test helper, applied to every backend package: for each plugin, assert connect({...valid, <plausible-typo>: 1}) rejects, driving the typo list from each backend's own key list (e.g. drop a trailing 's', swap in a sibling backend's key such as poll_interval_ms or db_path) so new keys are covered automatically.

summary: Comments across this file are addressed to reviewers and carry issue/bug identifiers rather than warning a future developer off a risky action, which CLAUDE.md rules out explicitly ('history belongs in the commit message, where it cannot rot against the code').
failure: Not a runtime failure. Instances: index.ts:126 'Blocking fetchRecent waiters keyed by NOTIFY channel (issue #20)'; :150 'SEC-06: warn loudly...'; :316 '(issue #20)' twice more; :420 'LISTEN before we register (BUG-29)'; :548 'A disconnect() can complete fully while connect() is in flight (BUG-16)'; :556 '(issue #20)'; :77 '(issue: lost wakeup)'. A reader six months out cannot resolve BUG-16/BUG-29/SEC-06 to anything in the tree, and the identifiers will outlive the code they annotate.
remediation: Strip the identifiers and keep only the risk-shaped remainder ('keep X, so that Y'); the issue numbers and the reasoning already live in commits f3f8c3d and c2901eb, which is where a reader looks for history.
testUpgrade: CLASS = comments that narrate history or address a reviewer. Extend packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts (which already walks every source file) with a case asserting no comment in packages/** matches /\b(BUG|SEC|FIX)-\d+|issue #\d+|as (the )?reviewer|per review\b/i - a repo-wide, self-widening guard rather than a per-file fix.

summary: `eventToMessage` forwards the raw, untrusted `content.body` JSON value into `buildMessage`; a non-string body from any room member throws inside `fetchRecent` and permanently bricks startup catch-up.
failure: Any member of the topic room (in `shared_room` mode any member at all; in per-topic mode any invited or federated participant) sends `PUT /rooms/<id>/send/m.room.message/<txn>` with `{"msgtype":"m.text","body":42}` — `body` is member-controlled JSON and Synapse enforces no schema on it. Reproduced against the in-package fake: `fetchRecent({topic, limit:10})` rejects with `TypeError: content.matchAll is not a function` (thrown by core's `parseMentions`, reached via `buildMessage`), and `catchUpTopic` rejects with `catch-up failed on topic "hostile2" while resuming from the stored cursor "$e0:fake"`. Because `buildBridge` awaits `catchUpAll`, every subsequent restart fails the same way until the read-state file is hand-edited — exactly the failure mode BUG-10 was fixed for. On the live path the same event is instead silently swallowed by `deliver`'s catch, so one hostile event is a hard DoS on catch-up and an invisible drop on push.
remediation: Coerce and bound the inbound field where it crosses the seam: in `eventToMessage` use `typeof e.content?.body === 'string' ? e.content.body : ''` (and likewise guard `sender`/`origin_server_ts`), or skip the event entirely. The durable fix belongs in `bridge-core`'s `buildMessage`, which should reject or coerce a non-string `content` rather than letting `parseMentions` throw — every HTTP backend has this shape (`bridge-slack/src/index.ts:630`, `bridge-discord/src/index.ts:700` read remote JSON the same way). Also stop `deliver` from silently swallowing the same class on the push path.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any remote JSON field a backend reads must not be able to throw out of `fetchRecent`/`subscribe`. Add a table-driven case in packages/bridge-matrix/test/catchup-sync.fake.test.ts that pushes a hostile event for each malformed shape — `body` as number, object, array, boolean, null, missing; `content` missing entirely; `sender` missing; `origin_server_ts` as a string/NaN — crossed with both `shared_room` and per-topic mode and with all three read paths (`fetchRecent` no-since, `fetchRecent` since, `subscribe`), asserting each path resolves without throwing and that `catchUpTopic` still advances. Widen `FakeSynapse` with an `addHostile(content: unknown)` injector so the generator can emit arbitrary content. The existing tests only ever construct events via `addMessage`/`post`, which always produce a string body, so the guard could never fire.

summary: `blockingFetch` fires `driveBoundedSync` with `void` and runs its reconciling `fetchSince` re-query without waiting for that sync's `timeout=0` positioning to complete, so a message landing in that window is seen by neither and the call idles the whole `blockMs`.
failure: No `subscribe` loop covers the (room, topic), so `blockingFetch` takes the dedicated-sync branch. `void this.driveBoundedSync(...)` (line 423) issues a `timeout=0` positioning `/sync` whose `next_batch` will be taken at time T'; the re-query at line 431 is issued concurrently and served at time T. A belonging message landing between T and T' is behind the re-query and before the positioning token, so the incremental syncs never report it. Reproduced with the fake's `positioningDelays=1 / positioningDelayMs=400`: post at t=120ms, `fetchRecent({since: tail, blockMs: 3000})` returned the message only at t=3010ms (the deadline), not at ~150ms. With core's default `catchup.block_max_ms` of 60s that is a landed message invisible for a full minute. This is the mirror of the fix already applied to `subscribe`, which correctly adds to `liveTopics` only after positioning is awaited (lines 577-581).
remediation: Have `driveBoundedSync` return (or resolve) a `positioned` promise once the `timeout=0` sync's `next_batch` is in hand, and `await` it in `blockingFetch` before issuing the reconciling `fetchSince` at line 431 — mirroring the `liveTopics`-after-positioning discipline in `subscribe`. Keep the deadline clamp so the await cannot overrun `blockMs`.
testUpgrade: CLASS: for every wake source, the reconciling re-query must be ordered strictly after the source is positioned. Parameterize packages/bridge-matrix/test/wake-source.fake.test.ts over WHICH positioning sync is stalled — {none, the subscribe loop's, the blocking fetch's own, both} x {shared_room, per-topic} x {no subscribe, subscribed to the blocked topic, subscribed to another topic} — with the message landing inside the stall window, asserting the fetch returns the message in well under `blockMs`. That needs a `FakeSynapse` stall selector keyed on request ordinal or filter rather than the current global `positioningDelays` counter, which today is always consumed by the first (subscribe) positioning sync and therefore never exercises the dedicated path.

summary: `deliveredBelonging` is set only in the fresh-events loop, so belonging messages delivered through the `limited`-burst `backfill` recovery never call `wakeRoomWaiters` and a parked long-poll on that exact (room, topic) sleeps out its whole budget.
failure: shared_room mode, `subscribe('topic-A')` running, a blocking `fetchRecent({topic:'topic-A', since: tail, blockMs: 3000})` parked (it takes the `liveTopics` branch and opens NO dedicated sync, so the subscribe loop is its only wake source). A burst lands where the belonging message is older than the per-sync cap and the newest `cap` events are all foreign-topic: `timeline.limited === true`, `backfill` recovers the belonging event and `deliver`s it, but `deliveredBelonging` stays false (lines 627-638), so `wakeRoomWaiters` at line 642 is never called. Reproduced with the fake (`syncCap = 2`, then add [A:'fresh', other:'f1', other:'f2'] at t=150ms): the live handler received 'fresh' at ~150ms while `fetchRecent` returned it only at t=3012ms, the full budget. Production `block_max_ms` default 60s.
remediation: Set `deliveredBelonging = true` inside the `for (const e of recovered)` loop (or call `this.wakeRoomWaiters(roomId, topic)` unconditionally after any delivery). Better still, wake from a single `deliver` helper so no future delivery path can be added without waking, rather than from a flag that each call site must remember to set.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every path that hands a message to the subscribe handler must also wake parked waiters. Add a parameterized case in wake-source.fake.test.ts over DELIVERY PATH — {normal incremental sync, `limited` burst recovered via `prev_batch` backfill, mixed burst where the belonging event is in the truncated tail} x {shared_room, per-topic} — with `syncCap` driven from the table, asserting both that the handler saw the message and that a concurrently parked `fetchRecent({blockMs})` returned it within a small multiple of the observed live-delivery latency. A cheap structural ratchet: assert `waiters` is empty immediately after each live delivery. The existing BUG-09 burst test asserts only handler delivery and never parks a waiter.

summary: If the reconciling `fetchSince` re-query throws, `blockingFetch` propagates the rejection without waking the waiter, leaving an armed timer, a registered waiter and a live dedicated `/sync` behind for the rest of `blockMs`.
failure: `const recheck = await this.fetchSince(roomId, topic, sinceCursor, limit);` (line 431) and the post-park `fetchSince` (line 439) are not wrapped in try/finally. A transient homeserver 500 or a socket reset makes `this.http` throw; `fetchRecent` rejects, but `waiter` stays in `this.waiters`, its `setTimeout(waiter.wake, remaining)` keeps the event loop alive, and `driveBoundedSync` keeps long-polling until the timer eventually fires — up to `catchup.block_max_ms` (60s default) of orphaned work per failed call. Under a flapping homeserver these accumulate.
remediation: Wrap the body of each loop iteration from waiter registration onward in `try { … } finally { waiter.wake(); }` (wake is already idempotent and self-cleaning), so any throw tears down the timer, the registration and the dedicated `/sync` before propagating.
testUpgrade: CLASS: an error thrown anywhere inside a blocking/parking primitive must leave no timer, no registration and no in-flight request. Add a fault-injection table to catchup-sync.fake.test.ts that makes `/messages` fail on the Nth call for N in {the pre-park recheck, the post-park re-query} x {HTTP 500, network reject}, asserts `fetchRecent` rejects, and then asserts the private `waiters` and `controllers` maps are empty and that no pending timers remain (e.g. via vi.useFakeTimers() + vi.getTimerCount() === 0). No existing test injects a `/messages` failure at all — the resilience suite only injects `/sync` failures.

summary: The comment above the re-query claims it closes the lost-wakeup window "for BOTH paths", explicitly naming the dedicated sync's `timeout=0` positioning — a guarantee the code does not provide, as the reproduced race above shows.
failure: Lines 426-430 read: "Close the lost-wakeup window for BOTH paths: a belonging message may have landed between the caller's first `fetchSince` and the wake source being armed (… before `driveBoundedSync`'s `timeout=0` positioning for the dedicated one). Re-check ONCE now that the waiter is live across the snapshot". The re-query is issued concurrently with, not after, that positioning sync, so the dedicated path's window is left open — demonstrated by a 3010ms return on a 3000ms budget. A future developer reading this comment will conclude the window is handled and not look for the race; the JSDoc on `blockingFetch` (lines 353-362) and on `waiters` (lines 140-146) repeat the same claim.
remediation: Fix the code (await positioning before the re-query) and then delete the explanatory prose entirely — once the ordering is expressed by an `await`, the comment restates the code and earns no place under CLAUDE.md's comment rule. If any note survives, phrase it as the risk: "keep the positioning await before the re-query, so that a message landing in the positioning window is not lost."
testUpgrade: CLASS: a comment asserting a concurrency guarantee must have a test that fails when the guarantee is removed. For each such claim in this file (waiter-registered-before-arming, positioned-before-registering in `subscribe`, re-query-after-arming) there should be a named test whose failure message quotes the claim; enforce by mutation — reordering the two statements the comment describes must turn the suite red. The `subscribe` positioning claim passes this bar today; the `blockingFetch` one does not.

summary: The `concurrently, while its own positioning sync is still in flight` row stalls only the subscribe loop's positioning sync, so the case named for the blocking fetch's own positioning window never actually exercises it.
failure: `fake.positioningDelays = 1` is a global counter consumed by the FIRST `timeout=0` sync issued, and the test's own comment states this is the subscribe loop's. In the `no subscribe` variant the row is `continue`d, and in the two subscribed variants the blocking fetch's own positioning sync is never delayed — so the row's name promises coverage of the dedicated-sync positioning window while the assertion can only ever observe the `liveTopics` branch. Setting `positioningDelays = 1` before the blocking fetch with no subscribe at all (the cell the table excludes) makes the same assertion fail at 3010ms — the defect the row is named after is live and green.
remediation: Give `FakeSynapse` a targeted stall (by request ordinal, or by a predicate on the request URL/filter) instead of a global first-N counter, and add the `no subscribe` x `own positioning in flight` cell that the table currently skips.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a fixture's fault injection must be attributable to a specific participant, or the case silently grades the wrong one. Replace the `positioningDelays` counter with `stallPositioning: (n: number) => boolean` (or a per-caller tag) and make the wake-source table iterate an explicit `stallTarget` dimension {none, subscribe-loop, blocking-fetch, both}; record and assert on which request was actually stalled, so a row that stalls nobody fails loudly instead of passing.

summary: `disconnect()` stops the subscribe loop only via the shared `stopped` flag, so a `connect()` that lands while a loop is parked in its retry backoff resurrects it with a stale `nextBatch`, room id and handler.
failure: Traced, not reproduced (core's stdio-bridge.ts:68 calls `connect` once per process, so this is latent). Sequence: `/sync` fails, the loop is inside `await delay(syncRetryDelayMs(n))`; `disconnect()` sets `stopped = true` and clears `liveTopics`/`controllers`; `connect()` sets `stopped = false` and mints a new token. The parked loop then re-enters `while (!this.stopped)`, resumes against the OLD `nextBatch` for the OLD room with the OLD handler, and — since `liveTopics` was cleared — is invisible to `blockingFetch`'s wake-source choice. A second `subscribe()` after reconnect yields two loops delivering into two handlers.
remediation: Replace the boolean with a monotonic generation counter incremented by `connect`/`disconnect`; capture it when the loop starts and exit when it no longer matches. Same guard for `driveBoundedSync` and the `fetchWithRetry` `isStopped` callback.
testUpgrade: CLASS: no background loop may outlive the `disconnect()` that stopped it, including across a subsequent `connect()`. Add a lifecycle table exercised against every long-running primitive (subscribe loop, dedicated bounded sync, 429 retry backoff): drive each into its wait, `disconnect()`, `connect()`, then assert the fake recorded zero further requests attributable to the pre-disconnect generation and that a handler registered before the disconnect receives nothing afterwards. Parameterize over WHERE the loop was parked when the disconnect landed {in-flight sync, retry backoff, hot-spin pacing delay}.

summary: `post()` puts caller content verbatim into an XML `<body>`; a C0 control character is illegal in XML 1.0, so the server kills the stream with `not-well-formed`, destroying every non-persistent MUC room the bridge occupies and with it the MAM archive of EVERY topic — not just the one posted to.
failure:
Reproduced against the dev-compose Prosody (packages/bridge-xmpp/dist/index.js): post(t1,'topic1-history'); post(t2,'topic2-history'); fetchRecent(t1)=['topic1-history'], fetchRecent(t2)=['topic2-history']. Then post(t1, 'x'+String.fromCharCode(1)) three times ->
  [parley-xmpp] stream error: not-well-formed
  evil post 0/1/2 FAILED: reconnected; retry post
  t1 after []   t2 after []
One message from one topic silently wiped the archive of an unrelated topic, the rejection blames 'reconnected; retry post' (inviting the retry that repeats the damage), and each retry kills the stream again. `content` reaches the plugin unvalidated — core's tool schema is a bare `z.string()` (packages/bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:228).
remediation: Validate/normalise `content` in `post()` before serialising: reject (fail-fast, with an error naming the offending codepoint) or strip codepoints XML 1.0 forbids — C0 except \t \n \r, lone surrogates, U+FFFE/U+FFFF. Do the same for `nick` and any other config-derived string that lands on the wire. Do not rely on the server for input validation, and never let a content-shaped error surface as a generic reconnect message.
testUpgrade: Table-driven `post()` case over a generator of XML-hostile payloads — every C0 control, a lone high surrogate, a lone low surrogate, U+FFFE, U+FFFF, a NUL, and (as negative controls) \t/\n/\r and astral emoji — asserting for each that either the post resolves and round-trips through fetchRecent, or it rejects with an error naming the codepoint, and in BOTH cases that a subsequent fetchRecent on an untouched second topic still returns its prior history (i.e. the stream survived). Existing conformance 'post -> fetchRecent' only ever posts ASCII, so it cannot see this class.

summary: After a single live wake that the MAM query cannot satisfy, `parkCap` is latched to 50 ms for the rest of the call and never reset, converting a long-poll into a 50 ms archive-query loop for the whole remaining budget; and because the waiter timer is armed BEFORE the query, a server RTT above 50 ms makes the rounds fully back-to-back.
failure: Reproduced with the in-package fake (test/fake-xmpp.ts, `reflectOnly` — the exact 'live stanza the archive does not hold' case the suite's own long-poll-wake.test.ts models): fetchRecent({since: tail, blockMs: 600}) with one reflectOnly at t=50 ms issues MAM queries at t=3,51,102,153,204,255,305,354,404,454,505,556,602 — 12 archive queries for one blocked fetch. Scaled to core's default catchup.block_max_ms=60_000 that is ~1200 MAM IQs per blocked fetch_recent, per agent, per topic, against a shared server. With blockMs=2000 I measured 41 queries; the existing 'spurious wake re-arms instead of returning early' test asserts only elapsed>=380 ms and so stays green through the storm.
remediation: Bound the lag re-poll instead of latching it: reset `parkCap` to Infinity when a capped round wakes with 'timeout' (the lag window is over), or cap only a small fixed number of re-polls after each 'message' wake. Separately, arm the waiter timer for the park AFTER the query returns (keep the waiter *registration* before the query — that is what closes the lost wakeup — but start its timer at park time) so the cadence is a real 50 ms rather than max(0, 50-RTT).
testUpgrade: Parameterized long-poll case over (mamLatencyMs x blockMs x wake-pattern: none / one spurious / one lagging-then-archived / repeated spurious), counting `onMamRequest` invocations and asserting a bound of the form ceil(blockMs / MAM_LAG_POLL_MS) is NOT reached — e.g. queries <= 4 for a single non-productive wake, at every latency. Guards the whole class of 'a wake latches a poll cadence' regardless of which knob a later refactor moves.

summary: `onErrorMessage` falls through to reject the room's pending JOIN whenever a `<message type='error'>` bounce matches no pending post — so a delayed bounce for an already-cleared post rejects an unrelated, still-unanswered join with the post's condition, which is not in RETRYABLE_CONDITIONS.
failure: Reproduced with the fake: post in flight -> `pendingPosts.clear()` (exactly what connect()'s reconnect `online` handler does at index.ts:241-242) -> `joinOnce(room)` in flight (what the same handler drives at :248) -> the server's bounce for the pre-reconnect post arrives. Result: `MUC join error (not-acceptable: no voice) for t-cross@muc.parley.local`, pendingJoins drained to 0, while the server has not answered the join presence at all. `not-acceptable` is not retryable, so doJoin gives up, ensureJoined drops the cache, and push for that topic stays dead until some later post/fetchRecent happens to re-drive it — with a diagnostics line blaming the join for a post's error. The existing error-stanza.test.ts only covers a WRONG-ROOM bounce, never a wrong-KIND one, so it stays green.
remediation: Only settle the join from a message bounce when the stanza actually correlates to a join attempt (no origin-id / no id, or an id the plugin minted for the join). An error bounce whose origin-id matches nothing should be logged and dropped, not applied to whichever correlator happens to share the room key.
testUpgrade: Extend the correlator-provenance table from 'right token, wrong sender' to 'right room, wrong operation kind': for each pair (join in flight, post in flight, long-poll waiter armed, MAM collector open) feed the error/result/reflection stanza belonging to the OTHER kind on the same room and assert nothing settles, with the matching-kind stanza as the negative control in every row.

summary: README: 'The Parley bridge stays joined to every topic it serves, so rooms it serves never empty' — false. Any stream drop ends occupancy instantly, destroying every non-persistent room and its whole MAM archive, and the reconnect handler re-joins only rooms in `subscriptions`, never rooms joined via post/fetchRecent.
failure: Same live Prosody reproduction as the control-char finding, but the doc claim is independent of the trigger: after one stream drop, `fetchRecent(t1)` and `fetchRecent(t2)` both returned `[]` where they had returned their history seconds earlier. Neither topic was subscribed, so index.ts:244 re-joined nothing; even a subscribed room is destroyed at the instant the stream drops, before any re-join can run. The README frames persistent rooms as needed only 'for history that must survive a full bridge restart', so an operator following it loses all history on any network blip.
remediation: Correct the note: state that MAM history survives only if the MUC service defaults rooms persistent (or rooms are pre-created persistent), because any stream reconnect — not just a restart — empties a non-persistent room. Consider making the plugin re-join every room in `joined` (not only subscribed ones) after reconnect, and/or warning at connect when the served rooms are non-persistent.
testUpgrade: A live-server test (skipIf no server, like cursor-inputs.test.ts) parameterized over {subscribed, catch-up-only} topics that posts, forces a stream drop (`priv(plugin).xmpp.stop()`/emit reconnect), waits for re-join, and asserts fetchRecent still returns the pre-drop history — the case that fails today and pins whichever claim the README ends up making. Plus a unit assertion that the reconnect handler re-drives every key in `joined`, not just `subscriptions`.

summary: `post()` accepts and silently discards `opts.inReplyTo` (`_opts`), with no JSDoc and no README note — the one backend that neither implements threading nor declares that it doesn't.
failure: post(topic, handle, 'reply', { inReplyTo: someId }) returns a normal top-level message id; the threading relation is dropped with no error, no log, no doc. Every other plugin honours it — bridge-discord:221, bridge-matrix:219, bridge-nats:136, bridge-postgres:244, bridge-redis:241, bridge-slack:196, bridge-sqlite:171, bridge-telegram:218 — and bridge-zulip, which also drops it, at least states so in its JSDoc (bridge-zulip/src/index.ts:204). XMPP has XEP-0461 `<reply to= id=>` available, so the omission is a choice presented as if the parameter were honoured.
remediation: Either emit XEP-0461 `<reply>` (plus XEP-0201 `<thread>`) when `inReplyTo` is set, or keep dropping it and say so — a JSDoc on `post` and a README row, in the same shape as the existing 'identity is not used' blockquote — so the divergence is visible rather than silent.
testUpgrade: A cross-backend conformance case (in packages/conformance) that posts with `inReplyTo` and asserts each plugin either surfaces the relation on the fetched message or advertises the limitation through a declared capability flag on the context — turning 'silently ignored seam option' into a suite-level check instead of a per-plugin reading exercise. Guards the class for every future backend, not just XMPP.

summary: `subscribe` detects an out-of-band stream recreation (compares `StreamInfo.created` and resets `lastSeq`), but `readRecent` has no equivalent check. JetStream sequences restart at 1 in the recreated stream, so a persisted cursor from the old stream is permanently past the new tail and `fetchRecent` returns an empty page with `nextCursor === since` forever. The catch-up path goes silently and permanently deaf while `post` and `subscribe` on the same topic keep working.
failure: Live probe against nats:2.10 `-js`: post 'before-1','before-2' to topic `recreate` -> fetchRecent returns cursor `2`. `jsm.streams.delete('PB_<tag>_recreate')` (exactly the out-of-band removal `withStream`/`ensureStream` exist to survive). post 'after-1' -> stream re-provisioned, seq 1. `fetchRecent({topic, since: '2'})` -> `{messages: [], nextCursor: '2'}`; repeated -> `{messages: [], nextCursor: '2'}`. 'after-1' is never returned to catch-up, and the cursor never advances no matter how many messages are subsequently posted (until seq climbs back past 2).
remediation: Give `readRecent` the same recreation guard `subscribe` already has: cache the stream's `created` timestamp per topic (or re-read it on the `startSeq > lastSeq` branch) and, when `Number(since) > lastSeq` and the stream's `created` differs from the one the cursor was minted under (or unconditionally when `since` exceeds `last_seq`, which is unreachable for a cursor this plugin actually minted), fall back to `startSeq = firstSeq` and return the available window rather than an empty page. Whatever the policy, it must not be 'stall forever'.
testUpgrade: Class = 'the backend store was re-provisioned under a persisted cursor'. Add a parameterized case to the shared conformance suite (packages/conformance/src/index.ts) driven by an optional `ctx.reprovisionStore(topic)` hook, running the table {post N -> read cursor -> reprovision -> post M} x {catch-up via fetchRecent(since), live via subscribe} and asserting every post-reprovision message is eventually observed on BOTH paths and that the cursor strictly advances. The existing packages/bridge-nats/test/resource.test.ts 'post and fetchRecent still work after the stream is deleted out-of-band' is too narrow: it calls `fetchRecent({topic})` with NO `since`, which is exactly the shape that cannot fail — widen it to replay the pre-deletion `nextCursor`.

summary: `since` is caller-controlled (the `parley_fetch_recent` MCP tool declares it as `z.string().optional()`), and the plugin feeds it straight into `Number()` and then into `opt_start_seq` with no validation that it is a cursor this plugin could have minted. Non-integer and non-numeric values split into two bad outcomes: a silent permanently-empty page, or an opaque JetStream error. Both violate fail-fast; the first is silent wrong output.
failure: Live probe, topic `junkcursor` containing one message at seq 1. `fetchRecent({since:'1e999'})` -> `{messages: [], nextCursor: '1e999'}` — Number('1e999')=Infinity, `startSeq > lastSeq` is true forever, so the existing message is never returned and the cursor never advances, on every subsequent call, for the life of the topic. `since:'1.5'` -> same permanent empty (startSeq 2.5). `since:'0x2'` -> silently accepted as 2. `since:' 1 '` -> works but echoes `nextCursor: ' 1 '` (whitespace preserved). `since:'abc'` and `since:'-1'` -> throw `NatsError: consumer delivery policy is deliver by start sequence, but optional start sequence is not set`, an error that tells the caller nothing about the real cause.
remediation: Validate at the top of `readRecent`: if `since !== undefined` and it does not match `/^\d+$/` or is not a safe integer, throw a typed, self-describing error (e.g. `Error('invalid nats cursor: <value> — expected a JetStream sequence number')`). Do the same in `blockingFetch`. Never echo an unvalidated `since` back as `nextCursor`.
testUpgrade: Class = 'a cursor the plugin did not mint'. Add a parameterized conformance case `for (const bad of ['', ' 1 ', 'abc', '-1', '1.5', '1e999', '0x2', '99999999999999999999', 'null', '{}'])` asserting `fetchRecent({topic, since: bad})` either throws a typed error OR returns messages — but never returns an empty page whose `nextCursor` equals the malformed input while the topic demonstrably has messages. Widen the generator to fuzz arbitrary strings for the invariant 'empty page => a later call with a growing stream eventually returns messages'. No existing test in packages/bridge-nats/test or packages/conformance passes any non-plugin-minted `since`.

summary: `want = Math.min(limit, lastSeq - startSeq + 1)` assumes the sequence range is dense. After JetStream prunes the front of a stream (the `retention_days`/`max_age` feature this plugin ships), `first_seq` advances but a `since` older than it still yields `startSeq < first_seq`, so `want` over-counts by the pruned amount. The pull `fetch` then waits out the whole `FETCH_EXPIRY_MS` (2s) waiting for messages that will never exist, on every such call.
failure: Live probe: 20 messages posted to topic `gap`, then `jsm.streams.purge(stream, {seq: 11})` (first_seq=11, last_seq=20, messages=10). `fetchRecent({topic, since:'0'})` -> 10 messages, correct cursor 20, but **2009 ms**. The same read with `since:'15'` (inside the live window) took 4 ms and the no-`since` read took 5 ms. A bridge resuming after downtime longer than `retention_days` pays a flat 2s per catch-up page until its cursor climbs back inside the window.
remediation: Clamp with the count the server already reported: `want = Math.min(limit, Math.max(0, lastSeq - startSeq + 1), info.state.messages)`, and/or raise `startSeq` to `Math.max(startSeq, firstSeq)` when `since` predates the retained window (the messages in the gap are gone either way, so nothing is skipped that still exists).
testUpgrade: Class = 'the sequence range is not dense'. Parameterized test over {no prune, prune below `since`, prune above `since`, prune everything} x {no-since, since-inside-window, since-before-first_seq}, asserting BOTH the returned set and that the call completes well under FETCH_EXPIRY_MS. The fake in packages/bridge-nats/test/fake-jetstream.ts cannot express this today — its `info()` derives `first_seq` from `records[0]` and its `fetch` returns immediately rather than modelling expiry — so widen the fake with an `expiryMs` that a short window actually waits out, which is what makes the defect observable.

summary: `retention_days` is passed to `streams.add` as `max_age` with no validation. `0` — the most natural way an operator writes 'do not retain' — is not `undefined`, so it sets `max_age: 0`, which JetStream defines as UNLIMITED: the config says 'keep nothing' and the stream keeps everything forever. A negative value fails late, at the first `post`, with an unrelated JetStream error.
failure: Live probe. `backend_config: { retention_days: 0 }` -> stream created with `max_age = 0` (JetStream: no age limit) — i.e. the exact opposite of what the value reads as, silently. `backend_config: { retention_days: -1 }` -> first `post()` throws `NatsError: duplicates window can not be negative`, an error naming a field the operator never set, at run time rather than at connect/config load.

summary: A subscribe push loop parked in `backoff()`'s `delay` survives `disconnect()` and resumes after a later `connect()`, delivering messages to a handler whose subscription was torn down.
failure: subscribe(t, h) → force /events to 500 for ~2.5s so the loop enters a multi-second backoff → disconnect() → connect() → post(t,'after-disconnect'). The old handler `h` fires again (probe observed got.length 2 vs expected 1). Cancellation is a single plugin-wide `this.stopped`, and `connect()` sets `this.stopped = false` (line 153), so any loop sitting in `await delay(...)` re-enters `while (!this.stopped)` with the stale `state.queueId`, gets BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID, re-registers a queue that is no longer in `this.queues` (so the next disconnect leaks it server-side), gap-fills from `lastDeliveredId` and replays into the dead handler. This violates the seam contract `disconnect(): Tear down the connection and ALL subscriptions` and the README's `disconnect() aborts in-flight polls`.
remediation: Bind each loop to a connection generation instead of the shared flag: capture `const gen = this.generation` at subscribe time (incremented by `connect()` and `disconnect()`), and make every loop predicate `gen === this.generation && !this.stopped`. Make `backoff()` abort-aware (race `delay` against an AbortSignal fired by disconnect) so teardown is prompt, and have `disconnect()` await the loop promises before resolving so no handler can fire after it returns.
testUpgrade: Parameterized 'loop cancellation survives teardown at every await point' table: for each place the loop can be parked — {events long-poll, failure backoff after 500, backoff after re-register failure, mid gap-fill, gap-fill retry backoff} × {disconnect only, disconnect+reconnect} — assert (a) zero handler invocations after `disconnect()` resolves, and (b) `fake.requestCount('POST /api/v1/register')` stops growing. Existing `operability.test.ts` 'disconnect completes in bounded time' only checks that disconnect *resolves*, never that the loop is actually dead.

summary: The entire blocking-fetch piggyback wake mechanism is unguarded: two mutations that destroy it — including the exact round-1 lost-wakeup shape — leave all 88 tests green.
failure: Mutation A: replace the body of `if (sawMessage) { const live = this.waiters.get(topic); ... wake(); }` (src/index.ts:509) with a no-op, deleting the wake edge entirely → `npx vitest run packages/bridge-zulip` = 88 passed. Mutation B: in `blockingFetch` (src/index.ts:265) re-query history FIRST and call `armSubscriptionWaiter` AFTER, reintroducing the arm-after-requery lost-wakeup that round 1 fixed → 88 passed. No test in the package ever exercises the piggyback branch (`this.waiters.has(topic)` true): `subscribe-race.test.ts`'s 'never parks on a dead subscription' table only covers subscribe() having FAILED, and the conformance blockMs case never subscribes, so it always takes the dedicated-queue path.
remediation: Add a piggyback-path table: subscribe(t) first, then run the blocking-fetch assertions against a live loop, asserting the wake latency (< 500ms for a 5000ms blockMs) — which kills mutation A — and inject the message at each handshake window relative to the waiter registration (via `fake.setResponseHook`) to kill mutation B.
testUpgrade: Parameterize on the CLASS 'a blocked fetchRecent wakes from whatever primitive is available': rows = {no subscription (dedicated queue), one live loop (piggyback), two live loops on the same topic, loop exits mid-wait, disconnect mid-wait}, each × {message injected before arming, after arming, during the re-check} using the response hook. Every row asserts both the returned messages and that the wait was < 25% of blockMs. Add a mutation gate to CI for this file so deleting the wake block or reordering the arm fails.

summary: `waiters` advertises a topic as piggyback-able whenever a loop exists, but wakes are only fired from the events-poll branch — so a blocking `fetchRecent` parks for its full `blockMs` whenever the loop is in failure backoff, re-registering, or retrying a gap-fill.
failure: subscribe(t) → `fake.failRoute('GET /api/v1/events', {status: 500})` so the loop is in backoff → `fetchRecent({topic: t, since: tail, blockMs: 3000})` with a post 100ms in. Measured elapsed 3010ms (the whole budget) instead of ~100ms; the message is only found by the post-timeout re-query. With core's default `catchup.block_max_ms` of 60000 this is a 600x latency regression on every `fetch_recent` for the duration of any transient backend hiccup — and core's `fetchRecentBlocking` cannot compensate, because the plugin consumed the entire deadline (blocking-fetch.ts:61 returns immediately once `now() >= deadline`).
remediation: Make the piggyback decision reflect whether the loop can actually wake anyone: track a `polling` flag on `TopicWaiters` set only while the events long-poll is in flight, and in `blockingFetch` fall back to `waitViaDedicatedQueue` when the loop is not polling. Alternatively fire the topic's wakes from `gapFill`'s per-page progress and after every recovery step, and cap the piggyback wait so a non-progressing loop degrades to the dedicated queue.
testUpgrade: Parameterized 'blocking fetchRecent wakes promptly whatever state the subscribe loop is in' table: rows = {healthy polling, /events returning 500, /events returning a non-queue 400, queue GC'd and re-registering, gap-fill history read failing N times, loop already exited}. Each row asserts the wake landed in < 25% of blockMs and returned the message. This generator would also have caught the finding above, since it forces the piggyback branch.

summary: `connect()` validates nothing; `events_timeout_ms: 0` (or negative) turns the push loop into an unthrottled, unlogged request flood against the operator's own Zulip.
failure: `connect({ site_url, events_timeout_ms: 0 })` then `subscribe(t, h)`: the abort timer fires immediately after each poll starts, the catch sees `capped === true` and RESETS `consecutiveFailures` to 0 (src/index.ts:463) so backoff and the stderr report never engage. Measured 770 `GET /api/v1/events` requests in 1 second, silently, forever. `0` is exactly the value an operator would pick to mean 'no client-side cap'. Same for negative values. `site_url` and `stream` are equally unvalidated: `stream: ''` posts to `to=''` and `site_url: 'not-a-url'` makes every request throw `Failed to parse URL` at first use rather than at connect.
remediation: Validate in `connect()` and fail fast: reject non-positive / non-finite `events_timeout_ms` (or clamp to a documented floor and say so in the README), reject a non-absolute `site_url` and an empty `stream`. Independently, floor the effective poll cap (e.g. `Math.max(1000, cfg.events_timeout_ms ?? 25000)`) so no config value can produce a zero-delay loop, and do not reset `consecutiveFailures` on a cap that fired sooner than the configured interval.
testUpgrade: Parameterized 'no backend_config value produces a hot loop or a deferred crash' table over `{events_timeout_ms: 0, -1, 0.5, NaN, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER}` × `{site_url: '', 'not-a-url', 'http://h/'}` × `{stream: '', 'parley'}`: each row asserts either `connect()` rejects with a message naming the offending key, or after 1s of subscription `fake.requestCount('GET /api/v1/events') < 20`. Reusable across every HTTP backend that has a poll-cap knob.

summary: The fake never emits a 429, so the Zulip-specific `retry-after` JSON-body parser the `http()` JSDoc advertises is entirely unexercised — and it also silently defeats the shared clamp.
failure: No code path in `fake-zulip.ts` produces status 429 and no test in the package mentions 429, so `readRetryAfter` (src/index.ts:743) has zero coverage. Rewriting it to `return 0` or dropping the `retry-after` body read keeps 88/88 green, yet the JSDoc claims 'transparently retries on 429 honoring Retry-After (header, or the retry-after JSON field — Zulip sends both)'. The function also never returns `undefined`, so `fetchWithRetry`'s `?? retryAfterFromHeader(res)` fallback and `clampBackoff`'s default are dead, and it re-implements the clamp locally (`Math.min(x, 5000)`) — a second copy that can drift from `MAX_BACKOFF_MS`.
remediation: Give the fake a `rateLimit(route, {times, headerSeconds?, bodySeconds?})` lever and cover the matrix. Make `readRetryAfter` return `undefined` when neither source is usable so the shared `clampBackoff`/`retryAfterFromHeader` path in net-util owns the default and the ceiling.
testUpgrade: Parameterized '429 retry honours the hint and is bounded' table: rows = {header only, JSON body only, both (header wins), neither, absurd 3600s value, 429 forever}, each asserting the observed inter-request gap ∈ [expected, MAX_BACKOFF_MS] and that a permanently-429 route terminates with a thrown error rather than looping. Run the same table against every backend using `fetchWithRetry`, since each supplies its own `retryAfterOf`.

summary: The optional real-server conformance run silently skips when `PARLEY_ZULIP_*` are set but the server is unreachable, and reports a skip reason telling you to set the variables you already set.

testUpgrade: Parameterized 'opt-in integration gate' table over `{no vars, partial vars, all vars + reachable, all vars + unreachable, all vars + 401}` asserting the run is respectively skipped / fails naming the missing var / runs / fails naming the URL / fails naming auth. Same class exists in every backend's optional real-server block, so put the gate helper in `@sharptrick/parley-conformance` and table it once.
